A First World War statute giving the President sweeping control over trade and property involving enemy countries and nationals. Between 1933 and 1977 its Section 5(b) also applied in declared peacetime emergencies and became the all-purpose economic sanctions authority.

::: {.official-links}
**Read the law** (official GovInfo text)

[Enacted text: 40 Stat. 411](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/statute/40/411){.btn-official} [Current U.S. Code: 50 U.S.C. 4301-4341](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/50/4305?link-type=html){.btn-official}
:::

## Key provisions

- Sec. 5(b): power to regulate or prohibit transactions in foreign exchange and property in which a foreign country or national has an interest.
- Authority to seize and vest enemy property.
- 1977 amendment: confined Sec. 5(b) to wartime while allowing existing programs to be extended one year at a time.

## Why it matters

It is the ancestor of modern sanctions law. Congress moved peacetime powers into [IEEPA](ieepa-1977.qmd), and the surviving Cuba program was later frozen in place by the [Helms-Burton Act](helms-burton-1996.qmd).

## Current status

In force, limited since 1977 to time of war, with pre-1977 programs grandfathered. The Cuba embargo regulations continue under it through an annual presidential extension.

## Where it sits

- **Layer.** Framework statute. Standing laws that create institutions or general procedures other laws and executive actions plug into, such as the National Security Act, the War Powers Resolution, IEEPA, and FISA. ([How the layers work](../study/index.qmd#the-authority-stack))
- **Builds on.** [Declarations of War](declarations-of-war.qmd).
- **Built upon by.** [IEEPA](ieepa-1977.qmd), [Helms-Burton Act](helms-burton-1996.qmd).
- **Codified in.** [Title 50 U.S.C.](title50-usc.qmd).
- **Era.** Civil War to the First World War ([timeline](../study/timeline.qmd)).
- **Study.** [Unit 4: Emergency and economic powers](../study/units/emergencies-sanctions.qmd) (core reading).
